name: Activist
summary: A concentrated equity strategy that takes a significant, usually non-controlling stake in one listed company and uses that position to push management for operational, capital-allocation or governance change that releases trapped value. It turns on two things: is there a specific, fixable cause of the discount in management's own decisions, and can a stake of the size activists actually take, typically under 10% of the target's shares, be built and held within the mandate?

pros.text: The alpha comes from change the activist helps cause rather than from a market, sector or factor forecast being right. The position itself is unhedged long equity, so the total return still carries full market and sector beta.

The discount has a named, fixable cause in management's own decisions: agency problems and poor decisions leave value trapped, which an engaged owner can release. That is the rationale the LOS asks for.
Tactics escalate, so the manager can open with private engagement and only pay for public pressure or a proxy fight if the board resists.
Influence is reached without buying the company: activists aim at their goals with stakes typically under 10% rather than pursuing a full takeover bid.

cons.text: Concentration risk: bottom-up and activist portfolios hold few names, so a single position can dominate results.
Liquidity risk: activist stakes, like the small-cap positions these managers often hold, can be hard to exit without moving the price.

It is costly and resource-heavy: success requires substantial resources to build the stake and make a credible case, and those costs are sunk before anything changes, which is why activism is dominated by specialist funds.
The evidence is mixed and situation-dependent: activism tends to add value where the target genuinely suffers from agency problems and poor decisions, less so where management was already competent.
Free-rider problem: engagement is costly for the engager while the benefits accrue to all holders, so the activist alone funds a campaign whose gains it cannot keep.

A successful campaign leaves a riskier company: revenue and earnings growth, profitability and governance indicators generally improve, but financial leverage at target companies rises significantly after activist involvement, so the stake still held is a more levered equity than the one bought.
A board seat can put material non-public information in the manager's hands and restrict its own trading in the name.

Unlike the market-neutral and statistical-arbitrage strategies in the same reading, activism carries no offsetting short: the stake stays a long, directional equity position for the years a campaign can run.

whenToRecommend: The vignette describes a target with underperforming operations or stock, excess cash or an otherwise inefficient balance sheet, poor capital allocation, weak governance, and a price below the sum of its parts.
The mandate tolerates very low breadth: a handful of holdings, each large enough in its own target for the demand to be credible, with board seats and public campaigns not prohibited.
The client has a multi-year horizon and no near-term call on the money, so a campaign can run to its conclusion.

The portfolio already has its broad market and factor exposure, the committee has room for more equity beta and single-name concentration, and what it wants on top is idiosyncratic, campaign-driven alpha rather than another factor tilt. Say explicitly that the sleeve adds beta as well as alpha; if the committee wants a diversifier instead, see whenNotTo.
The mandate can live with the publicity that stake building triggers: activist stakes are generally made public, and stakes above a jurisdictional threshold must be disclosed in most jurisdictions.
whenNotTo: The IPS limits how much of any one issuer the fund may own, or the fund is too small relative to plausible targets to reach a meaningful stake. Watch the denominator: influence is a percentage of the TARGET's shares, not of portfolio assets, so convert the limit into dollars and compare it with target market capitalisations before ruling activism out. Where no meaningful holding in a target is reachable, factor investing or a long/short sleeve takes the active risk instead.

The client may need the money within months. An activist stake cannot be sold quickly without moving the price, so an index-replication core fits the horizon; if active risk is still wanted, check the vehicle's redemption terms before treating any alternative as the liquid one.
Operations, capital allocation and governance are all sound and the only complaint is the price. There is no lever for a campaign to pull, so the case is a bottom-up value holding.

The committee wants a diversifier for an already equity-heavy portfolio. Activism is long, directional equity and the activist hedge fund index carries equity-like volatility, so a market-neutral strategy is what strips the beta out.

The investor cannot accept being restricted from trading by receiving non-public information. The campaign then has to run from outside the boardroom: voting, shareholder resolutions and public pressure rather than a board seat.

The thesis cannot be executed without control: the plan requires owning and running the business, or taking it private, rather than persuading a board. That points to private equity. Note what does NOT point there: demands to replace management or to change the capital structure are activist tactics, pursued with a minority stake and, if the board resists, a proxy fight.
pitfalls: Confusing activist with bottom-up. Both are concentrated and high-conviction, and the difference is the return source: bottom-up waits for the market to reprice the shares, the activist causes the change.
Writing that the horizon is long and stopping there. A campaign can run for years, yet an activist's horizon is typically shorter than a buy-and-hold investor's. Say both.

Attaching model risk or crowded-trade risk to activism. Those are the quantitative and statistical-arbitrage pitfalls. The risks named for activist and bottom-up portfolios are concentration and liquidity.

Answering 'it is undervalued' when asked for the characteristics of an activist target. Name three of these five: underperforming operations or stock, excess cash or an inefficient balance sheet, poor capital allocation, weak governance, a valuation below the sum of the parts.

Listing the tactics flat. Write the three types of demand, in the order the exam-focus line gives them: operational and strategic (cost cuts, asset sales, spin-offs, a sale of the company), then capital allocation (dividends, buybacks, a change in investment or M&A policy), then governance (board seats, replacing management, better incentives) up to a proxy fight if the board resists. The pressure escalates too, from private engagement to public campaign.

Skipping the middle of the process when the question asks for it. The sequence runs: identify the target, buy the stock, study the corporate structure, governance and shareholder base, submit a proposal to management, and if there is no agreement THREATEN a proxy contest and negotiate a settlement; only if that fails does an actual proxy contest go to a shareholder vote. The threat and the settlement sit between the failed private approach and a real contest, and leaving them out loses marks.

Giving the case against activism without short-termism and greenmail. Critics charge that SOME activists pursue short-term gains, a quick buyback or sale, at the expense of long-run investment, and that historically abusive tactics such as greenmail, buying a stake to pressure the company into repurchasing it at a premium, harmed the holders left behind.

cues.signal: A fund holds eight positions, the largest is 18% of assets, and it has asked for two board seats.
cues.implication: The board-seat request is what identifies activism. The concentration does not: the reading puts activist and bottom-up in the same breadth bucket, so eight high-conviction names are equally consistent with a concentrated bottom-up fund. The risks to discuss are concentration and liquidity, not model or crowding risk.

cues.signal: The company holds net cash worth a third of its market capitalisation and trades below the sum of its parts.
cues.implication: Two of the five target characteristics are present, which rules in a capital-allocation demand: a buyback, a special dividend or a spin-off. Look for the other three, operational underperformance, poor capital allocation and weak governance, before committing to the activist label. Whether the portfolio should instead be run as an index or factor mandate turns on the mandate and its constraints, not on this company's balance sheet.

cues.signal: The board has rejected two private approaches and the manager is weighing a public campaign.
cues.implication: Private engagement has failed, so the live options are public pressure and a credible THREAT of a proxy contest, which can end in a negotiated settlement with board seats conceded without a vote, and only if the board still resists, an actual proxy contest and a shareholder vote. The answer turns on the cost of escalation and the support of other holders, not on more valuation work.

cues.signal: The IPS forbids the fund from owning more than 2% of any issuer's outstanding shares.
cues.implication: This is the limit that bites, because it is denominated in the target's shares: 2% is far below the sub-10% stake activists typically need, so the demand cannot be made credible and activism is ruled out. Factor investing or long/short supplies the active risk within the limit. A cap on a holding's weight in the PORTFOLIO would not support the same inference.

cues.signal: Trustees require that the portfolio can be liquidated within one quarter if the mandate is terminated.
cues.implication: An activist stake is sized against the target's trading volume, not the fund's, and activists traditionally target small- and mid-cap names, so a disclosed stake is hard to exit inside a quarter without moving the price. The liquidity constraint weighs heavily and has to be addressed explicitly before any recommendation; check the stake against the name's daily volume rather than asserting the strategy is simply impossible.

cues.signal: Two other large shareholders have publicly backed the campaign.
cues.implication: Shareholder support is one of the three success conditions, alongside building a stake and making a credible case, and it is what turns a proxy threat into a real one. It is not sufficient: proxy contests are decided by votes, so check the company's defenses, since a staggered board, multi-class shares or a poison pill can blunt the threat whatever the public support. On balance it argues for pressing the campaign rather than abandoning the position.

cues.signal: The committee praises management's operating record but thinks the shares are cheap.
cues.implication: There is no governance or capital-allocation failure for a campaign to fix, so activism is the wrong label for this position. The vignette is describing a bottom-up value holding.

cues.signal: The IPS commits the fund to long-horizon stewardship and objects to pressuring companies for near-term payouts.
cues.implication: The short-termism criticism is the one to cite, and it rules out the quick-buyback-or-sale variety of campaign. It does not rule out activism as such: activism is engagement intensified rather than its opposite, its opening rung is private dialogue with the board, and the curriculum recognises an activist goal that is a non-financial cause such as an ESG issue. The fit is a long-horizon campaign on governance and capital allocation that stops short of demanding near-term payouts.

deleted: Repair pass: 'No crowding risk of the factor or stat-arb kind' as a pro: an absolute claim, and activists do crowd into the same disclosed names. The defensible half survives as the pitfall about which strategy family owns crowding risk.

Repair pass: 'Engagement yields insight into strategy, culture and the competitive environment': cited to overview_of_equity_portfolio_management, whose only evidence sentence here is about public campaigns, and as a general benefit of stewardship it is not a reason to choose activism over a sibling strategy.

Skeptic pass: the pro that a minority stake avoids paying a control premium, and that 'any re-rating accrues to the whole holding'. Both lenses flagged it. 'Control premium' appears nowhere in the candidate's material (a grep of CFAL3/Resources returns one hit, in the playbook itself), the curriculum runs the other way (the stock appreciates while the activist accumulates and adds about 2% on announcement, per Maug 1998 and the market-reaction box), and the second clause is the free-rider con restated as a benefit while the entry also asserts the con. Replaced with the grounded version of the same contrast: stakes typically under 10% rather than a full takeover bid.

Skeptic pass: the pro that 'the activist supplies its own catalyst'. Lens 2 called it the third rendering of one idea and Lens 1 agreed the pros were triplicated; 'catalyst' appears nowhere in the notes. The two lenses disagreed about which of the three to keep, and the grounded one won: pros 2 is the LOS's own rationale sentence, verbatim in the notes, so it stayed and the catalyst framing went.

Skeptic pass: the cue about having to stop trading the shares on taking a board seat. Lens 2 showed the inside-information point held three of the entry's slots (a con, this cue, and a whenNotTo bullet) while two facts the curriculum states outright were missing. One instance kept, as the con; the whenNotTo bullet kept because it is a genuine IPS constraint; this cue deleted and the leverage increase given a slot instead.

Skeptic pass: 'and it creates conflicts of interest' from the board-seat con. Vague with no conflict named, and misattached: the conflicts-of-interest cost is grounded in the overview reading's engagement economics (with a named example in the index-based reading), not as a consequence of a board seat in the active equity reading. Cut here rather than re-sited, to avoid padding.
corrected: Repair pass: Cue 3 called a public campaign 'the escalation ladder at its last rung, the proxy fight'. A public campaign is not the proxy fight; the proxy fight is the rung after it.

Repair pass: Cue 7 read two supportive holders as proving 'all three success conditions are met'. Shareholder support is one of the three and says nothing about whether the stake is adequate or the case credible.
Repair pass: the free-rider con and the inside-information con were both cited to a reading that does not support them, and were re-sourced to 'curriculum'.
Repair pass: the liquidity con no longer says the problem is 'worse in small caps'; the grounding lists activist stakes and small-cap positions side by side rather than compounding them.
Repair pass: whenNotTo 3 and cue 8 no longer rest on the deleted mixed-evidence claim.
Repair pass: summary now states the stake is significant but usually non-controlling, which is the dividing line against private equity.
Repair pass: confidence lowered from high to medium.
Repair pass: added a stewardship cue, where the short-termism criticism becomes the deciding point.

REVERSED (skeptic pass): the repair pass deleted 'the evidence that activism adds value is mixed and situation-dependent' as 'an empirical literature verdict with nothing behind it in the grounding'. Both lenses showed the rationale is false, and reading_notes.json reading 19 LOS 5 carries it verbatim, with the exam-focus line ending 'value-add is situation-dependent'. Restored as a con with the conditional that makes it examinable. The HFRX figures (Sharpe 0.56 against the S&P 500's 0.54, on too few managers to conclude) corroborate it but are left out of the item so its reading source stays honest; they are in los_drills_r20 q4.

REVERSED (skeptic pass): the repair pass dropped 'which is why activism is dominated by specialist funds' from the cost con as 'an empirical claim with no grounding'. Also false: the notes read 'Success also requires substantial resources, a credible threat, and the support of other shareholders, which is why activism is dominated by specialist funds.' Clause restored.

REVERSED (skeptic pass): the repair pass recorded that 'pitfall 5 invented an escalation order by type of demand (operational, then capital allocation, then governance)'. The three demand categories are the notes' own ordered bullets under 'Activist TACTICS escalate from private engagement to public pressure', and the exam-focus line repeats them as the thing to write. Restored as the list, with the private-to-public pressure ladder kept as the second axis.

REVERSED (skeptic pass): the free-rider con is back on overview_of_equity_portfolio_management, not 'curriculum'. Neither lens caught this; checking the repair pass's other provenance calls turned it up. That reading's notes carry 'Benefits accrue to ALL holders, which creates the free-rider problem: engagement is costly for the engager and its gains are shared', in a passage that places 'activism at the far end' of engagement. The inside-information con stays 'curriculum', correctly: material non-public information language appears only in the ethics readings.

CAUSE OF THE THREE REVERSALS ABOVE: grounding.json's slice for this key is an incomplete extract (15 sentences) of reading_notes.json reading 19 LOS 5. It omits the rationale sentence, the target-characteristics sentence, the three tactic bullets and the whole 'case for and against activism' paragraph. The repair pass read those gaps as absence of support. Every claim in this version was re-checked against reading_notes.json, flashcards.json, los_drills_r20 (LOS e) and los_drills_r6 (LOS d) rather than against grounding.json.

Skeptic pass: both lenses found the same denominator error in three places, and it is now fixed in all three. whenNotTo 1 said 'the IPS caps any single holding at a few percent of assets. A stake that small buys no influence'; the cue signal was '5% of portfolio assets'; the summary asked whether 'the mandate can hold a stake large enough'. An IPS cap is a percentage of the PORTFOLIO; influence is a percentage of the TARGET. A USD 10bn fund under a 5% cap can commit USD 500m, which is 25% of a USD 2bn company, and a few percent of a company is the normal activist stake, not one that buys no influence. The cue signal is recast as an issuer-ownership cap, whenNotTo 1 now says to convert the limit and compare it with target market caps, and the summary quantifies the stake as typically under 10% of the target's shares.

Skeptic pass: both lenses flagged whenNotTo 6, which filed 'a recapitalisation and a change of management' on the private equity side. Both are curriculum-listed activist tactics (los_drills_r20 q1 lists 'changes to management, changes to the capital structure'; the notes' governance bullet reads 'seek board seats, replace management'). The bullet now keeps only the genuine dividing line, needing to own and run the business, and says explicitly that those two markers do not point to private equity.

Skeptic pass: both lenses flagged pros 1 for claiming performance 'does not depend on a market, sector or factor forecast being right', which contradicted the entry's own con that activism hedges nothing. Narrowed to the alpha source, with the beta of the position stated.

Skeptic pass: both lenses flagged cue 7's 'support from other holders is the one of the three success conditions the activist cannot buy'. It contradicted the cost con, the curriculum tactics include 'coordinate with other shareholders' and running a media campaign, and the sentence was ungrammatical. Rewritten, with Lens 1's addition that proxy contests are decided by votes, so the company's defenses (staggered board, multi-class shares, poison pill) can blunt the threat whatever the support.

Skeptic pass: both lenses flagged cue 9 for opposing engagement to activism. los_drills_r6 q7 defines activist investing as 'a distinct and specialized version of engagement' and the overview notes place 'activism at the far end' of engagement; los_drills_r20 q7 records that an activist goal may be 'a non-financial cause (e.g., environmental, social, and governance issues)'. The cue now scopes the criticism to the quick-payout variety of campaign and points a stewardship IPS at long-horizon, ESG-capable activism.

Skeptic pass: both lenses flagged the process gap in cue 3 and pitfall 5. Exhibit 19 (los_drills_r20 q8) puts 'threaten proxy contest' and 'negotiate settlement' between the failed proposal and an actual contest. Cue 3 now names the threat and the settlement, and a pitfall covers the full sequence, since the LOS asks for 'associated processes'.

Skeptic pass: Lens 1 showed whenToRecommend 4 and whenNotTo 4 reached opposite answers from nearly the same fact pattern, distinguished only by the word 'diversifier'. whenToRecommend 4 now states that the sleeve adds equity beta and single-name concentration as well as alpha, and cross-refers to whenNotTo.

Skeptic pass: Lens 2 showed whenToRecommend 5 was circular (recommend activism when the manager is capable of activism) and duplicated the cost con in the positive. Replaced with a real mandate condition the entry lacked: tolerance for the public disclosure that stake building triggers.

Skeptic pass: Lens 2 showed the 'it hedges nothing' con was cited to active_equity_investing_strategies, which discusses hedging only in the factor LOS and market neutrality only in stat-arb. Re-sourced to 'curriculum' and reworded as the contrast with the market-neutral and stat-arb strategies in the same reading, which is the grounded half.

Skeptic pass: Lens 2 showed the cost con's 'all of which must be paid for before anything changes' overstated the notes and contradicted cue 7. The costs clause now covers building the stake and making the case, not rallying holders.

Skeptic pass: pitfall 4 asked for three characteristics and then listed four, merged two of the notes' five, and dropped 'or stock' from 'underperforming operations or stock'. Now 'name three of these five', with the five as the notes give them.

Skeptic pass: both lenses, each at low confidence, flagged cue 5 for asserting an activist stake 'cannot' be exited in a quarter. Softened to the comparison the grader expects, the stake against the name's trading volume, while keeping the direction of the answer and the point that activists traditionally target small and mid caps.

Skeptic pass: Lens 1 flagged whenNotTo 2 for offering a long/short sleeve as the liquidity remedy for money needed within months, since long/short is typically accessed through vehicles with notice periods and lock-ups. Trimmed to index replication, with a note to check redemption terms. (Long/short survives in whenNotTo 1, where the point is active risk inside an ownership cap, not liquidity.)

Skeptic pass: Lens 1 flagged cue 2 for concluding that one company's balance sheet 'rules out an index or factor answer'. That turns on the mandate, not the company. Non-sequitur removed, and the cue now says only two of the five target characteristics are present.

Skeptic pass: Lens 2 flagged cue 1 for presenting low breadth as part of the identification when the notes put activist and bottom-up in the same breadth bucket, which is the confusion pitfall 1 warns against. The board-seat request now does the identifying.

Skeptic pass: two facts the curriculum states outright and the entry omitted are now in, both called for by skeptic fixes: financial leverage at target companies rises significantly after activist involvement (a con, so a successful campaign leaves a more levered equity), and the activist goal may be a non-financial ESG cause (in the stewardship cue).
Skeptic pass: the short-termism pitfall now says 'SOME activists', as the notes scope it, rather than attributing short-termism to the strategy.
Skeptic pass: pros went from five to four and one cue was deleted; nothing was added to replace them beyond the two grounded facts named above. Confidence stays medium.
_review.residualRisk: Two things to double check. First, the board-seat con is general Level III knowledge rather than material from this reading: material non-public information language appears nowhere in the active equity notes, flashcards or drills, only in the ethics readings, so it is sourced 'curriculum' and kept once rather than three times. Lens 2 raised it at low confidence and the inference is sound, but it is inference. Second, grounding.json's slice for this key is an incomplete extract of the candidate's notes, and it is what misled the repair pass into three false 'no grounding' deletions. Any later pass on this entry should validate against reading_notes.json reading 19 LOS 5, flashcards.json (fc_active_equity_investing_strategies_007 parts 1 to 10) and los_drills_r20 LOS e, not against grounding.json. Also noted: the HFRX activist index figures and the 2% announcement reaction are grounded in the drills but appear nowhere in this entry, having been judged padding once the claims they were brought in to qualify were deleted.
